meta.title: Who really said "If each of us hires people who are smaller than we are, we shall become a company of dwarfs. But if each of us hires people who are bigger than we are, we shall become a company of giants"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — David Ogilvy, in Ogilvy on Advertising (1983). It was the note he folded inside a Russian nesting doll and mailed to every new office head.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1911–1999 · British advertising executive, founder of Ogilvy & Mather
answer.sourceLine: Ogilvy set this down in Ogilvy on Advertising (1983), describing a habit: when someone was made head of an office in the Ogilvy & Mather chain, he sent them a Matrioshka doll from Gorky, and this message was folded inside the smallest doll. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ transcribes the passage and cites page 47.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: A note folded inside a Russian nesting doll

source.excerpt: When someone is made the head of an office in the Ogilvy & Mather chain, I send him a Matrioshka doll from Gorky. If he has the curiosity to open it, and keep opening it until he comes to the inside of the smallest doll, he finds this message: If each of us hires people who are smaller than we are, we shall become a company of dwarfs. But if each of us hires people who are bigger than we are, we shall become a company of giants.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries the whole passage — doll, curiosity, message — and cites Ogilvy on Advertising, page 47. The sentence above is the message, verbatim.
The book was first published in 1983; the Internet Archive catalogues editions from 1983 and 1985 under Ogilvy on Advertising, all lending-restricted, so we could not read page 47 ourselves.

Neither Wikiquote ↗ nor Quote Investigator records any competing claimant, earlier appearance or disputed wording for this line — we searched Quote Investigator for it and it has no article on the quotation.
Wikipedia ↗ confirms Ogilvy founded Ogilvy & Mather, the chain of offices the passage is about.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed in Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗, citing Ogilvy on Advertising, page 47. The italics on dwarfs and giants are Ogilvy’s. We could not open the book — the Internet Archive’s copies are lending-restricted — so the page number is Wikiquote’s locator, not one we confirmed.

author.name: David Ogilvy
author.heading: About David Ogilvy
author.metaLine: 1911–1999 · British advertising executive, founder of Ogilvy & Mather
author.bio: David Mackenzie Ogilvy founded his advertising agency in New York in 1948 with $6,000 and financial backing from his brother Francis, then managing director of the London agency Mather & Crowther. By 1963 Ogilvy, Benson & Mather billed $55m across 19 clients, Rolls-Royce among them. Time called him “the most sought-after wizard in today’s advertising industry” in 1962, and he is widely called the father of advertising.

misattribution.heading: How it travels
misattribution.intro: The attribution is not contested. What goes missing is the doll.

items.why: The line is almost always quoted on its own, as a flat hiring rule. In the book it is the message folded inside a Russian nesting doll that Ogilvy mailed to each new office head — the doll is the argument, and the sentence is only its punchline.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Ogilvy’s own, in his own book. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ cites Ogilvy on Advertising, page 47.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Ogilvy founded his agency in New York in 1948 with $6,000 and backing from his brother Francis; by 1963 Ogilvy, Benson & Mather was billing $55m across 19 clients. By the time he wrote Ogilvy on Advertising the firm was a chain of offices, and the problem this passage addresses is what happens to a chain when each link hires defensively.

The delivery is the argument. A manager who does not open the doll never reads the message — Ogilvy says so in the passage, and makes curiosity the entry fee. A manager who does open it has already demonstrated the trait being asked for.
detailsBody: Matrioshka dolls — the nested Russian figures — were made at Gorky, now Nizhny Novgorod. Each doll contains a smaller one; Ogilvy’s point is that a company that hires downward does the same thing, one diminishing figure at a time.

A note on our sourcing: this record rests on Wikiquote’s sourced transcription rather than on the book, which we could not open from here. The page number, 47, is Wikiquote’s. Nothing we found contradicts it, and no other author has ever been credited with the line.
context.pull: If he has the curiosity to open it, and keep opening it until he comes to the inside of the smallest doll, he finds this message.
